title: Your Methods
intro: Try each method on your own material and keep the ones that work for you. Your own scores will tell you. These are your scores on Mnemos tasks.
caption: These are your scores on Mnemos tasks. A few attempts is not much to go on, and some of the change is simply learning the task.

fewAttempts.heading: Why a few attempts is not much to go on
fewAttempts.text: Your score on any one try depends on many things: how tired you were, how hard that material was, whether you knew the task already and plain luck. One or two tries can look good or bad for reasons that have nothing to do with the method. Scores settle down after several tries on different material. So read these as a rough guide to what is worth another go, not as a verdict. A method that scored lower today may still be one you like, and one that scored higher may not suit what you want to keep.

lowDataLine: With fewer than four tries, no comparison is shown yet. Keep trying and the picture will fill in.
keepWhatWorks: If one method keeps working for you on the kind of thing you want to keep, use it. If another feels better to you, use that. Both are fine. You can change your mind at any time.

alsoSay: Mnemos does not sort people into types. We try methods and look at what helps.
evidence: A major 2008 review found no adequate evidence base for matching teaching to a learning style, and almost no studies that tested the idea properly. So the game offers methods to try and your own scores to look at, and makes no claim about types.
source: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork 2008, Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 9(3), 105-119
